content: Rheumatic fever is a systemic immune-mediated disease that can develop following an infection caused by Streptococcus bacteria, such as strep throat or scarlet fever. This condition primarily affects the heart, joints, blood vessels, and brain. Rheumatic fever is classified as either acute or chronic, depending on the duration of symptoms. The most common cause of this disease is an infection with Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus. If left untreated, rheumatic fever can lead to valvular heart diseases, including mitral or aortic valve stenosis and regurgitation, as well as myocarditis. These complications can result in reduced cardiac output, pulmonary edema, and eventually heart failure. However, in cases without carditis, the prognosis is excellent, with no residual heart disease. Conversely, in patients with preexisting heart disease, the prognosis is poor and may result in mortality. Common complications of rheumatic fever include arrhythmias, systemic embolism, and stroke. Physical examination findings often include fever, cardiac murmurs, and erythema marginatum. Diagnostic tools such as echocardiography and chest radiographs are useful in identifying the disease. The Jones criteria are employed to confirm the diagnosis of rheumatic fever. Treatment typically involves antibiotics to eradicate the Streptococcus infection and anti-inflammatory medications, such as aspirin and corticosteroids, to reduce inflammation. Long-term penicillin prophylaxis is crucial to prevent recurrence and further complications. Rheumatic fever has been recognized since ancient times, with Hippocrates first describing it between 400 and 370 B.C. The term rheumatic fever was introduced in the early 1600s by Guillaume de Baillou, a French physician. In 1944, Dr. T. Duckett Jones published the first set of diagnostic criteria for the disease. The pathophysiology of rheumatic fever involves an autoimmune response triggered by a Streptococcus pyogenes infection in individuals who have been immunologically sensitized by prior infections. During the infection, antigen-presenting cells, such as macrophages, present bacterial antigens to helper T cells. These T cells then activate B cells, leading to the production of antibodies against the Streptococcus cell wall. However, these antibodies can also cross-react with the myocardium and joints, resulting in the clinical manifestations of rheumatic fever. The primary cause of rheumatic fever is an infection with Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes. It is important to differentiate rheumatic fever from other diseases that present with fever, skin rash, nausea, and fatigue, such as typhoid fever, malaria, Lassa fever, Ebola, and scarlet fever. The incidence of rheumatic fever has significantly declined in developed countries like the United States and Canada. Between 1970 and 1990, the incidence was approximately 20-40 cases per 100,000 individuals, but it has since decreased to 5-20 cases per 100,000 in Canada and fewer than 5 cases per 100,000 in the United States. Rheumatic heart disease is now rare in these regions. However, rheumatic fever remains endemic in many developing countries and is most commonly observed in children aged 5-15 years. Risk factors for developing rheumatic fever include low socioeconomic status, inadequate healthcare access, and poor sanitation. Screening for rheumatic fever is essential, as many cases of rheumatic heart disease are subclinical. Echocardiography is recommended for individuals in high-risk regions, and if abnormalities are detected, further cardiac evaluation and antimicrobial therapy are initiated. If untreated, rheumatic fever can progress to severe complications, including arrhythmias, systemic embolism, and endocarditis, which may lead to heart failure. Common complications include valvular stenosis, carditis, and stroke. The prognosis is generally poor without treatment. The Jones criteria are used to diagnose rheumatic fever. A definitive diagnosis requires evidence of a recent streptococcal infection, such as elevated or rising antistreptolysin O titers or DNAase levels, along with either two major criteria or one major and two minor criteria. A thorough patient history is critical for diagnosis, with a focus on prior rheumatic fever episodes, family history of the disease, and recent streptococcal infections. Common symptoms include fever, nosebleeds, and skin rashes. Physical examination findings often reveal fever, Sydenham's chorea, cardiac murmurs, and erythema marginatum. Laboratory findings may show elevated inflammatory markers, evidence of streptococcal infection, and increased antistreptolysin O antibody titers. Electrocardiograms may demonstrate PR interval prolongation, conduction abnormalities, arrhythmias, or P mitrale, depending on the extent of cardiac involvement. Chest X-rays may reveal cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema secondary to heart failure. Echocardiography is particularly useful for diagnosing carditis and monitoring valvular defects. The primary treatment for rheumatic fever involves antimicrobial therapy combined with anti-inflammatory medications. Penicillin is the drug of choice, although ampicillin and amoxicillin are equally effective. Supportive therapy includes the continuous use of low-dose antibiotics, such as penicillin, sulfadiazine, or erythromycin, to prevent recurrence. Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G and oral penicillin V are recommended for treating Group A streptococcal infections in patients without penicillin allergies. Secondary prevention involves initiating antibiotic prophylaxis immediately after completing the initial treatment for rheumatic fever. The duration of prophylaxis depends on the degree of cardiac damage caused by the disease.
